title: Putting It All Together
hook: What if your best notes become the thing that keeps you from hearing?
counterintuition: Prepared moves turn wooden when you perform them in order; choose what the live moment needs and let new information change you.
tryThisNow: Pick the avoided conversation and sketch the sequence: raise or let go, prepare, open, listen, speak, solve, close.
keyTakeaway: Use the full arc as preparation, not performance: decide whether to raise it, prepare, open well, listen, speak, solve if ready, and close clearly.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beatrice has a folded page of notes inside her canvas bag. The retention-risk email is real. The conference room clock is loud. The key designer across from her looks more tired than angry.

The moves only help when they make you sound like yourself, not like a script. Preparation gives you range. The live talk decides which move matters now: listen first, speak plainly, name the gap, solve later, or admit this talk cannot happen on hoped-for terms.
breakdown.deepRead:
Beatrice planned the full arc. Sort the three conversations. Check purpose. Open from the third story. Listen from the inside out. Speak from experience. Problem-solve when ready. Close with next steps. The notes are good. Then the designer says, "I do not think you actually want to know why I am leaving."

That sentence changes the order. If Beatrice performs her opener anyway, the method becomes a wall. The live move is listening first. She leaves the notes in the bag and asks, "What makes it feel that way?" Now the preparation is doing its real job. It helps her choose, not recite.

Openness to being changed is the skill underneath all the skills.

A complete difficult conversation has an arc, but the arc is not a formula. Sometimes you decide not to raise it because the purpose check fails. Sometimes you raise it and discover feelings need acknowledgment before facts. Sometimes the third-story opener works and then your internal voice gets loud. Sometimes expression is enough for today, and problem-solving would be premature. Sometimes action is needed, and warmth without next steps would be another form of avoidance.

Hold the AND. You can be prepared and surprised. You can be clear and wrong about part of your story. You can be kind and firm. You can listen without surrendering your view. You can name your contribution without taking all the blame. These pairings keep the conversation human when a checklist would make it mechanical.

A clean close is not relief; it is knowing what remains open and what happens next. Maybe the close is a next step with owner and date. Maybe it is an agreement to pause and return. Maybe it is an honest statement that the other person is not engaging and you will choose a different path.
breakdown.fullRead:
Anke hears the lab freezer humming behind the tense meeting and wants to swat away the old authorship issue. The agenda is about a new grant. The authorship spreadsheet is from last year. Still, every decision is bending around it. The old issue is not interrupting the real topic. It may be the real topic that never finished.

Putting the pieces together means choosing the move the moment requires. For Anke, the move is not problem-solving the grant yet. It is asking whether the previous conversation actually ended. For Pablo, trapped in a late-night text thread, the move is not a perfect written script. It is moving the conversation out of the thread and restarting from purpose, feeling, and listening on the front steps with the phone charger still in his pocket. For Elliot, facing one more declined invite from a senior leader, the move is not another brave invitation. It is documenting the pattern, consulting the HR contact, and accepting that silence has changed the available path.

A closing warning says the framework is not a script. They work only if they help you stay plain and real, not like someone reciting a procedure. If you use them to extract agreement, the other person will feel the extraction. If you use them to stay curious, accurate, and steady, the same moves sound plain.

In the 2010 supplement, the closing questions matter because real conversations often arrive with silence, power, history, or a screen between people. Non-engagement may mean the conversation cannot happen on the terms you hoped for. A large power gap may require allies, exits, documentation, or a third party before any elegant opener. Feelings that seem illegitimate are still feelings first; their logic can be examined later. Old issues may be old because they were never resolved. Written media can give you drafting time while also stripping tone, curiosity, and repair from the exchange.

What would it mean to be changed? Not defeated. Not converted. Changed. It might mean learning that your story missed an important fact. It might mean realizing the conversation is not safe enough to continue directly. It might mean hearing that your good intent had a bad effect. It might mean giving up the apology you wanted and choosing a cleaner boundary instead. The deeper skill is letting the other person's answer alter what you thought you knew.

Min sees the limit in the rehearsal room. Stage lights warm the empty floor while the schedule says she will meet the famous founder alone. Her first draft is a careful third-story opener about access in the arts collective. After one rehearsal, she sees the structure more clearly: the founder can decide access regardless of collaborative language. The next right move includes an ally text and exit options, not only better wording. Skill does not erase structure.

Hugo ends with a phone face down beside a handwritten plan and half-finished tea. He writes the three layers, the purpose, the opener, the listening reminder, and one possible next step. Then he makes the call. It will not go exactly as written. That is not failure. Preparation is there so he can stay oriented when reality answers back.

A clear close names the unfinished pieces and the next step. "We will think about it" may be enough if the next step is a pause with a date. "I hear you" may be enough if expression was the purpose. "I cannot keep trying this directly" may be enough if the other person will not engage. The point is not to master conversations so they stop being hard. The point is to stop letting their difficulty decide for you.

examples.title: Beatrice Leaves the Notes in the Bag

planSpec.domain: full arc for a strained team-lead conversation
planSpec.audience: readers needing the whole sequence without sounding scripted
planSpec.stakes: a key designer may quit if the team lead performs technique instead of being real
planSpec.requiredBeat: Beatrice works from preparation notes, then leaves them in her bag when the live conversation needs listening first

examples.scenario: What if the right opener is not the next right move? Beatrice has preparation notes folded inside a canvas bag, a retention-risk email, and the conference room clock ticking above the door. She must decide whether to recite her plan. When the designer starts with hurt, Beatrice leaves the notes in the bag and listens first.
examples.whatToDo: Use preparation to choose the live move. Beatrice should let the sequence change when the conversation clearly needs listening before her planned opener.
examples.whyItMatters: A complete plan can become performance. The skill is staying oriented without forcing the conversation through a fixed order.

examples.title: Anke Stops Swatting the Old Issue Away

planSpec.audience: students and researchers with recurring unfinished conflict
planSpec.stakes: an old authorship issue keeps entering every new decision
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anke stops swatting away the old issue and asks whether the previous conversation ever actually finished

examples.scenario: The lab freezer hums behind the tense meeting while an authorship spreadsheet sits under the new agenda. Anke has to choose between calling the old issue irrelevant and asking whether it ever actually finished. She pauses the grant decision and asks what from last year is still entering the room.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the returning issue as unfinished, not irrelevant. Anke should ask what remains unresolved before trying to solve the new agenda item.
examples.whyItMatters: Old issues often return because they were never closed. Swatting them away only pushes them into the next decision.

examples.title: Pablo Moves It off Text

planSpec.domain: partner conversation across text and in person
planSpec.audience: couples moving from risky written medium to live repair
planSpec.stakes: a late-night text thread has created tone neither person intended
planSpec.requiredBeat: Pablo moves the conversation out of the thread and restarts from purpose, feeling, and listening

examples.scenario: At 12:18 a.m. on the front steps, "This is getting worse by text," Luke writes while the text thread climbs and Pablo's phone charger drags across the concrete. Pablo must decide whether to perfect one more message. He stops typing and asks to talk live, then restarts with purpose, feeling, and a question.
examples.whatToDo: Change the medium when writing is worsening tone. Pablo should use text only to move toward a live repair, not to complete a delicate conversation by perfect wording.
examples.whyItMatters: Text gives drafting time but hides tone and curiosity. Moving live can restore the cues the conversation needs.

examples.title: Elliot Stops Forcing the Invitation

planSpec.domain: employee facing non-engagement from a senior leader
planSpec.audience: workers needing limits when the other person will not participate
planSpec.stakes: silence from the leader means the hoped-for talk cannot happen on hoped-for terms
planSpec.requiredBeat: Elliot documents the pattern and chooses a safer next move instead of forcing one more invitation

examples.scenario: At 8:05 a.m. at Elliot's desk, a calendar invite is declined without comment for the third time, and the notes file now has dates beside each attempt. Elliot must decide whether one more invitation would be courage or denial. He documents the pattern, saves the messages, and contacts HR to choose a safer next move.
examples.whatToDo: Recognize non-engagement as a limit. Elliot should stop treating the missing conversation as a personal failure and choose a path that does not require participation from the leader.
examples.whyItMatters: The moves assume some engagement. When silence is the response, documentation, advice, or a third party may be the available route.

examples.title: Min Adds an Ally and an Exit

planSpec.domain: friendship with large power gap in arts collective
planSpec.audience: creative communities where status changes the conversation
planSpec.stakes: a famous founder can decide access regardless of collaborative language
planSpec.requiredBeat: it takes Min one rehearsal to see she needs an ally and exit options, not only a better opener

examples.scenario: It took Min one rehearsal under warming stage lights to see the empty room more clearly. The rehearsal schedule, access badge, and ally text show a power gap her opener cannot erase. Before meeting the famous founder, she must decide whether to rely on wording alone or choose an ally, an exit option, and then the cleanest sentence she can safely use.
examples.whatToDo: Plan around structure, not only wording. Min should bring support and preserve exit options before relying on collaborative language.
examples.whyItMatters: Skill does not erase power. A better opener may help, but access and status can still decide what happens.

examples.title: Hugo Makes the Call

planSpec.audience: general readers turning the framework into one concrete act
planSpec.stakes: the conversation has been delayed long enough that avoidance now has its own cost
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hugo writes the three layers, purpose, opener, listening reminder, and one possible next step before making the call

examples.scenario: At 8:02 a.m., Hugo sets his phone face down beside a handwritten plan and half-finished tea. Before making the call, he writes the three layers, purpose, opener, listening reminder, and one possible next step. The call still changes shape, but avoidance no longer gets to decide.
examples.whatToDo: Prepare the arc, then act. Hugo should use the plan to stay oriented while leaving room for the other person's response to change the next move.
examples.whyItMatters: Abstract mastery is not the end. One real conversation, handled imperfectly but deliberately, is the transfer point.

questions.prompt: A team lead prepares a careful opener, but the employee begins with a hurt statement that clearly needs listening first. What should the lead do?
choices: Use the preparation to change order and listen before delivering the opener.
Deliver the planned opener anyway so the structure stays intact.
Skip the conversation because preparation failed.
questions.explanation: Preparation should create range, not rigidity. The live conversation is asking for listening before the planned entry.

questions.prompt: A lab group keeps saying an authorship complaint is old, but every new decision reactivates it. What integrated move fits best?
choices: Swat the old issue away so the current agenda can continue.
Ask whether the previous conversation actually finished before solving the new decision.
Move straight to next steps for the new grant.
questions.explanation: Old issues often return because they remain unfinished. Treating the authorship concern as live may be necessary before design can work.

questions.prompt: A late-night text thread keeps making tone worse. One partner wants to craft a perfect final message. What is the better move?
choices: Keep revising until no misunderstanding is possible.
Send a longer explanation with all feelings and facts.
Stop using text for the delicate part and move the repair to a live conversation.
questions.explanation: Writing can help draft, but it often hides tone and curiosity. When the medium is worsening the exchange, move the delicate work live.

questions.prompt: A senior leader repeatedly declines invitations without comment. The employee keeps thinking a better opener will solve it. What limit is showing?
choices: Non-engagement means the hoped-for conversation may not be available on hoped-for terms.
The employee has not memorized the sequence well enough.
All difficult conversations require more persistence.
questions.explanation: The moves assume some participation. Repeated silence may call for documentation, advice, or a third party rather than another invitation.

questions.prompt: A member of an arts collective prepares a collaborative opener for a famous founder who controls access. What should she add to the plan?
choices: A more elegant third-story sentence only.
An ally, exit options, and a realistic view of the power gap.
A promise to avoid mentioning the problem directly.
questions.explanation: Collaborative language cannot erase structural power. Support and exits may be as important as wording.

questions.prompt: Someone uses every move in order and sounds rehearsed. The other person feels managed rather than met. What went wrong?
choices: They used too few moves.
They should have skipped preparation entirely.
They treated the moves as a script instead of choosing what the moment required.
questions.explanation: Mechanical order can become performance. The moves should help the person sound clearer and more real, not like a procedure.

questions.prompt: A speaker learns mid-conversation that their story missed an important fact. What shows genuine openness to being changed?
choices: They update the story while keeping their experience and concern available.
They abandon the conversation because being wrong is embarrassing.
They force the original plan because changing course looks weak.
questions.explanation: Openness is not surrender. It means letting new information alter the story while still speaking honestly about what happened for you.

questions.prompt: A conversation ends with warmth but no agreement about what happens next, even though action is needed by Friday. How should the close be judged?
choices: Successful, because relief means the relationship improved.
Incomplete, because a close needs clarity about next steps or remaining open points.
Too practical, because difficult conversations should avoid logistics.
questions.explanation: Warmth can still drift. When action is needed, the close should name what remains open and what happens next.

questions.prompt: A person has been avoiding a conversation for months and keeps studying the moves instead of acting. What is the best next transfer step?
choices: Wait until they can guarantee the conversation will go well.
Drop the issue because preparation has taken too long.
Prepare the layers, purpose, opener, listening reminder, and one possible next step, then have the conversation.
questions.explanation: The point is not abstract mastery. A prepared, imperfect conversation is better than letting avoidance keep deciding.

reviewCards.front: Why is the full sequence not a script?
reviewCards.back: Because the live conversation decides which move is needed. Preparation helps you choose, not recite.

reviewCards.front: What skill sits underneath all the conversation moves?
reviewCards.back: Openness to being changed by what the other person says, while still holding your own experience clearly.

reviewCards.front: What should you do when the other person will not engage at all?
reviewCards.back: Recognize the limit. You may need to wait, document, seek advice, involve a third party, or choose another path.

reviewCards.front: Why do large power gaps require more than a better opener?
reviewCards.back: Because structure can decide outcomes regardless of collaborative language. Allies, exits, or external processes may be needed.
It names what is resolved, what remains open, and what happens next, even if the next step is a pause or a different route.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is composing from the full set of moves while staying real, responsive, and open to what changes in the room.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the other person starts somewhere unexpected, then use your preparation to choose the needed move instead of reciting the opener.
If an old issue keeps resurfacing, then ask whether it was ever actually finished before solving the new topic.
If text is making tone worse, then use writing only to move toward a live or richer conversation.
If the other person will not engage or holds much more power, then add documentation, allies, exits, or third-party support before relying on conversation skill.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one avoided conversation and write the sequence: raise or let go, purpose, opener, listening reminder, owned expression, possible next step.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, have one small conversation using preparation as orientation. Afterward, write what changed because the other person answered back.

Openness to being changed is the skill underneath all the skills.
A clean close is not relief; it is knowing what remains open and what happens next.
